question: A 12-year-old boy is referred to a pediatric neurologist because of repetitive motions such as blinking or tilting his head. He is brought in by his mother who says that he also clears his throat and hums repeatedly. These actions have been happening for the past year and his mother is concerned. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccinations and is meeting all developmental milestones. On physical exam, he shows no focal neurological deficits and is cognitively normal for his age. He occasionally sharply jerks his head to one side during the physical exam and utters obscene words. Which of the following is most associated with this condition?

options.opb: CAG repeat on the short arm of chromosome 4
options.opd: Severe atrophy of the caudate and putamen
options.ope: X-linked MECP2 mutation with female predominance

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Coprolalia -> Tourette syndrome -> 80% CHAIN: CAG repeat on the short arm of chromosome 4 -> Huntington's disease -> 70% CHAIN: Severe atrophy of the caudate and putamen -> Huntington's disease -> 80% CHAIN: 3 Hz spike-wave pattern on EEG -> Absence seizures -> 70% CHAIN: X-linked MECP2 mutation with female predominance -> Rett syndrome -> 80%
enhanced_information: Coprolalia is most associated with Tourette syndrome, not Huntington's disease or Rett syndrome. Therefore, the correct association is Coprolalia -> Tourette syndrome.
analysis: The presentation of repetitive motions such as blinking, head tilting, throat clearing, and humming, along with the occurrence of coprolalia (uttering obscene words), is highly suggestive of Tourette syndrome. Coprolalia is a hallmark symptom of Tourette syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by motor and vocal tics. The absence of severe neurological deficits, normal cognitive function, and the onset of symptoms during childhood further support this diagnosis. While the other options are associated with different conditions like absence seizures (3 Hz spike-wave pattern on EEG), Huntington's disease (CAG repeat on chromosome 4), and Rett syndrome (X-linked MECP2 mutation), coprolalia specifically points towards Tourette syndrome.
